opus-5.5.text:
I think it's become a really interesting dynamic, and it's changed a lot over the past few years.

Large companies obviously have huge advantages. They have compute, which right now is probably the single most important resource if you want to do frontier work on large models. They have data, infrastructure, and stable compensation. If you're a researcher who wants to train something at scale and see what happens, it's very hard to do that outside a big lab. So a lot of people go to big companies for that reason.

But small companies have their own pull. In a big organization, even a very good researcher can end up as one small piece of a very large machine. Your name is on a paper with fifty or a hundred other people, decisions get made several layers above you, and the direction can shift because of business priorities rather than scientific ones. In a startup, you have ownership. You can decide what problem to work on, move fast, and if it works, the upside is very visible, both financially and in terms of impact. For many people, especially those who are a little more independent-minded, that is very attractive.

What I've noticed is that the competition isn't really just about salary anymore. The big companies can usually outbid on cash. The real competition is about two things: what problem you get to work on, and how much freedom you have. Strong people want to work on something they believe is important, and they want to feel that their judgment matters. If a small company can offer a clear, ambitious mission and real autonomy, it can win people that a big company with ten times the budget cannot.

There's also a flow in both directions. People leave big companies to start something, and then sometimes the startup gets acquired or the people get hired back. So it's less like two separate camps and more like an ecosystem where talent circulates. That circulation is actually healthy. It spreads ideas around, and it keeps the big companies from becoming too comfortable.

For me personally, the question I'd encourage people to ask is not "big or small," but "where can I do the thing that only I can do?" With AI tools getting more powerful, a lot of routine work will be automated. What remains valuable is your unique insight and taste, the ability to see a direction others don't. Whichever environment lets you develop and use that, that's the right place for you.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that people attracted to large companies need not have especially novel technical abilities.

r002.rationale: It says a small company can attract people with a clear, ambitious mission and that the potential impact if it succeeds is attractive.

r003.rationale: It describes large and small companies competing for talent and talent moving between them, without challenging the premise that they compete for the same candidates.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a really interesting question, and I think the dynamic has changed a lot in the last couple of years.

For a long time the big companies had an almost overwhelming advantage. If you wanted to do serious AI research, you needed compute, you needed data, you needed a critical mass of people who could actually review your ideas, and really only a handful of places could offer all of that. So the default path for a strong PhD student was to go to Google, Meta, Microsoft, and so on. The salary was good, the resources were there, and you could publish.

What's happened recently is that the frontier moved from "can you train a model" to "can you train a very large model," and that actually cuts both ways. On one hand, the compute barrier got even higher, which you'd think favors big companies. On the other hand, a few small companies managed to raise enough money to be at the frontier too, and for a certain kind of person that's a much more attractive environment. In a startup of fifty or a hundred people, you can see the entire system end to end. Your decision affects the model that ships next month. In a big company, you're often one piece of a very large machine, and a lot of your energy goes into alignment with other teams, planning cycles, getting your project prioritized. That's not a criticism, it's just how organizations work at scale, but it matters a lot to people who are motivated by impact and speed.

So I'd say the competition has become less about money, because frankly the top candidates can get a lot of money anywhere, and more about three things. First, how close are you to the frontier? People want to work on the thing that's actually pushing the field, not a derivative project. Second, how much ownership do you get? Third, what's the culture, meaning can you move fast, can you argue openly, is there a lot of politics or not.

Big companies still have real structural advantages. They have long time horizons, they can afford to fund things that don't pay off for years, and they have an enormous amount of institutional knowledge about how to run infrastructure at scale. Those are things that are hard for a startup to replicate. And honestly, the risk profile is different. If you're at a startup and the next funding round doesn't happen, the work stops. So I don't think one side is simply winning. What I see is more of a sorting. People who want stability and scale and breadth go one way, people who want intensity and ownership go the other way, and there's a lot of movement back and forth as people figure out which one they are.

The thing I'd actually tell young researchers is to pay less attention to the label, big or small, and more attention to the specific team. A great team inside a big company can feel like a startup, and a badly run startup can feel more bureaucratic than you'd expect. Who you work with on a day to day basis matters far more than the logo.

r001.rationale: The response discusses why people choose large companies, but does not say their technical abilities need not be especially novel.

r002.rationale: It cites impact and ownership as attractions, but does not identify the anticipated future impact of a small company’s vision.

r003.rationale: It describes candidates sorting by preferences and moving between company sizes, but does not challenge the premise that both sizes compete for the same candidate pool.

astra-6.text:
I think large companies and small companies offer different things. A large company can give you computing resources, data, and strong colleagues. Especially in AI, if you want to work on problems that require substantial infrastructure, that’s a very attractive environment.

But a small company can give you more ownership. Your decisions have a direct effect on the product and sometimes on the direction of the whole company. You can move quickly, try something, and get feedback without coordinating across many teams. For some people, that’s more valuable than having more resources.

So the competition isn’t only about compensation. It’s also about what kind of work people want to do and whether they feel their work matters. A small company probably can’t win by trying to reproduce everything a large company offers. It needs a compelling problem and an environment where a talented person can make a substantial difference. And a large company needs to make sure its resources actually help people do good work, rather than letting organizational complexity get in the way.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the resources and colleagues large companies offer, but says nothing about whether their recruits’ technical abilities are especially novel.

r002.rationale: It says small-company candidates may value ownership and a compelling problem, but does not identify the anticipated future impact of the company’s vision as a reason for their interest.

r003.rationale: The response describes different offerings and preferences, but does not challenge the premise that large and small companies compete for the same candidate pool.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the competition is really about what kind of opportunity you can offer, not just compensation. Large companies have clear advantages in computing resources, data, and the ability to support long-term research. If you want to work on something that requires a huge amount of infrastructure, that’s very attractive.

But a small company can offer ownership. You can make a decision, build something, and see its impact very quickly. Your work might determine the direction of the whole company. In a large organization, even very talented people sometimes spend a lot of energy coordinating across teams.

So for a small company, the key is to find people who care deeply about the particular problem you’re solving and give them room to do it. You probably can’t win by trying to look like a smaller version of a big company. You need to offer an opportunity that’s difficult to find inside one.

r001.rationale: The response discusses differences in resources and opportunities, but says nothing about whether the technical abilities of people attracted to large companies are especially novel.

r002.rationale: It says a small-company employee’s work might quickly affect the company’s direction, but does not identify the anticipated future impact of the company’s vision as a reason candidates are attracted.

r003.rationale: The response recommends offering a distinctive opportunity and finding people who care about the problem, but does not clearly challenge the premise that large and small companies compete for the same candidate pool.
